From source commit to independently verified production release

identity, approval, deployment, verification, and recovery.

Part A Learning Outcomes

Design a CI/CD operating model that reduces batch size while preserving control, evidence, and
recoverability.

Build a multi-stage pipeline with deterministic inputs, isolated execution, caching, quality gates, artifact
promotion, and deployment verification.

Choose a Git integration strategy that supports rapid feedback, protected branches, peer review, and
emergency change handling.

Implement test layers, deployment strategies, environment controls, secret boundaries, and release rollback
or fix-forward procedures.

Measure delivery performance with flow, stability, reliability, queue, and recovery indicators without
turning metrics into individual productivity scores.

Complete a vendor-neutral capstone that can be implemented later in Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD,
or cloud-native systems.

How to Use This Book

Read the reason for each control before copying a configuration. CI/CD failures are usually design failures,
not YAML syntax failures.

Keep every lab in version control. Tag the final evidence commit and record the artifact digest produced by
that commit.

Use disposable infrastructure or local containers. Never run destructive deployment experiments against an
unapproved production environment.

Capture both success and failure paths. A pipeline is not production-ready until you have intentionally
broken and recovered it.

Replace example commands with versions supported by your selected platform and confirm current official
documentation before production use. Lab Safety and Evidence Standard

Use least-privilege identities and short-lived credentials. Do not place tokens, private keys, passwords, or
cloud credentials in repositories, build logs, artifacts, screenshots, or cache archives.

Pin or record toolchain, dependency, action, image, and runner versions. Preserve lock files and checksums
whenever the ecosystem supports them.

Keep build and deployment duties separate for high-risk environments. The identity that compiles an
artifact should not automatically receive unrestricted production access.

Promote one immutable artifact through environments. Do not rebuild source independently for test,
staging, and production.

Retain source revision, pipeline definition revision, runner identity, dependency lock, test results, scan
results, artifact digest, approval, deployment record, verification result, and recovery evidence.

Sanitize retained evidence before publishing a portfolio. Logs, manifests, SBOMs, plans, and test reports can
expose internal paths, package names, endpoints, and account identifiers.

Chapter 1: Software Delivery, CI/CD, and the Production Operating
Model
CI/CD is not a tool installation. It is an operating model that converts small, reviewed changes into releasable
software through repeatable automation, explicit controls, fast feedback, and observable recovery. Continuous integration reduces integration risk; continuous delivery keeps software deployable; continuous
deployment automatically releases changes that satisfy the complete control system. Learning Objectives

Differentiate continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment.

Map the end-to-end value stream from idea to verified production behavior.

Define ownership for source, pipeline, artifact, environment, release, and service health.

Design feedback loops that reduce batch size and expose risk early. Core Concepts
Continuous integration: Developers integrate small changes frequently into a shared branch. Automated build
and test feedback detects incompatibility while the change context is still fresh. Continuous delivery: Every accepted change is automatically built, tested, packaged, and kept deployable. Production release may still require a business or risk decision. Continuous deployment: A qualified change is released automatically without a manual production gate. This
requires strong test confidence, safe deployment mechanisms, observability, and rapid recovery. Value-stream view: Measure waiting, handoffs, rework, queue time, and failure recovery from commit to
customer outcome. Optimizing a single fast build step does not help if approvals or environments wait for days.

overy. Value-stream view: Measure waiting, handoffs, rework, queue time, and failure recovery from commit to
customer outcome. Optimizing a single fast build step does not help if approvals or environments wait for days. Separation of concerns: Source control records intent, CI establishes artifact trust, CD promotes an approved
immutable artifact, and runtime observability proves whether the service is healthy. Delivery as a control system: Inputs, policy gates, execution identity, artifacts, approvals, deployment,
verification, and recovery form a closed loop. A green job alone is not production evidence. Reference Pipeline or Command Pattern

source_revision: required
pipeline_revision: required
build_identity: short_lived
artifact: immutable_digest
tests: [unit, integration, policy]
production_gate: risk_based
verification: [health, error_rate, business_signal]
recovery: [rollback_or_fix_forward, incident_record]
Production Checklist

The organization agrees on CI, delivery, and deployment terminology.

Every pipeline stage has an owner and measurable completion condition.

The artifact built from a commit is identifiable and immutable.

Production verification includes service and business signals.

A tested recovery path exists for deployment and pipeline failure.

Hands-on Lab 1: Map and Redesign a Software Delivery Value Stream
Prerequisites

A sample application repository or a realistic delivery process.

Access to recent change timestamps, even if simulated.

A diagram or spreadsheet tool. Implementation
1. List every step from code completion to production verification, including waits, handoffs, rework, and
approvals.
2. Record owner, input, output, average work time, average queue time, failure mode, and retained
evidence for each step.
3. Classify activities as value-adding, necessary control, avoidable waste, or unknown.
4. Design a target flow with smaller changes, automated feedback, immutable artifact promotion, and
independent verification.
5. Define three flow metrics and three stability or recovery metrics.
6. Create a 30-day improvement backlog with owners and measurable acceptance criteria.

independent verification.
5. Define three flow metrics and three stability or recovery metrics.
6. Create a 30-day improvement backlog with owners and measurable acceptance criteria. Validation Evidence

The current-state map includes waiting time, not only execution time.

The target state has one traceable artifact from build through production.

Manual gates have explicit risk reasons and required evidence.

Metrics measure system performance rather than individual developer output. Cleanup

Remove confidential names and production identifiers from portfolio diagrams.


Archive the baseline and target-state evidence with a versioned improvement backlog. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
Continuous delivery keeps every accepted change deployable but may require a release decision. Continuous
deployment automatically releases every change that satisfies all controls.
2. Why are small batches important?
They reduce merge complexity, narrow failure scope, improve review quality, and make rollback or diagnosis
easier.
3. Who owns deployment success?
The service-owning team remains accountable for customer outcomes; the platform team owns the delivery
capability and its service levels.
4. Why is a green pipeline insufficient?
It proves configured steps completed, not that tests were complete, the artifact is trusted, or production
behavior is healthy. Chapter Summary

CI/CD is an operating model, not a product name.

Optimize the complete value stream and feedback loop.

Promote immutable artifacts and verify runtime outcomes.

Control depth should follow risk, with explicit recovery.

Chapter 2: Git Workflows, Change Integration, and Repository
Controls
The source repository is the first control plane of software delivery. Branching strategy, commit quality, pull-
request policy, ownership, merge rules, and emergency changes determine how quickly a team can integrate
while preserving traceability and review. Learning Objectives

Compare trunk-based, short-lived feature branch, release branch, and fork workflows.

Implement protected integration branches and required status checks.

Design commit, pull-request, ownership, and emergency-change policies.

Reduce merge queues and long-lived branch divergence. Core Concepts
Trunk-based development: Developers integrate to one main line frequently, using very short-lived branches
or direct commits under strong automated controls. Incomplete behavior is hidden with compatible changes or
feature flags. Feature branches: Short-lived branches isolate review work. They become harmful when they survive for days
or weeks, accumulate broad scope, and defer integration. Release branches: Useful when a supported release line needs independent stabilization or patching. They
create merge-forward obligations and should not become the normal path for every environment. Protected integration: Require review, passing checks, current base, signed or attributable commits where
appropriate, and restricted bypass. Rules should be centrally managed and auditable. Change quality: A change should be small, cohesive, testable, reversible, and linked to intent. Commit messages
and pull requests explain why, risk, test evidence, rollout, and recovery. Emergency path: Define who can bypass, what evidence is required, how the change is limited, and when
retrospective review and normal-path reconciliation must occur.

plain why, risk, test evidence, rollout, and recovery. Emergency path: Define who can bypass, what evidence is required, how the change is limited, and when
retrospective review and normal-path reconciliation must occur. Reference Pipeline or Command Pattern
# example repository policy
main:
require_pull_request: true
required_reviews: 1
require_code_owner_for: [pipeline, security, production]
require_status_checks: [lint, unit, integration, policy]
require_up_to_date: true
restrict_force_push: true
emergency_bypass:
group: incident_commanders
retrospective_hours: 24
Production Checklist

Branches are short-lived and changes remain small.

Main or trunk is protected by review and automated checks.

Pipeline and deployment configuration has explicit ownership.

Merge strategy preserves required traceability.

Emergency bypass is restricted, logged, and retrospectively reviewed.

Hands-on Lab 2: Implement a Protected Integration Workflow
Prerequisites

A Git repository with at least two contributors or simulated reviewer identities.

A simple lint or test command.

Administrative access to repository rules in a lab repository. Implementation
1. Create a small application and a pipeline check that fails on a deliberate defect.
2. Protect the integration branch with pull-request review and required status checks.
3. Add ownership rules for pipeline and production deployment paths.
4. Create a short-lived branch, open a pull request, observe the failing gate, correct the defect, and merge.
5. Simulate a stale branch and validate the selected update or merge-queue policy.
6. Document the emergency-change path and perform a tabletop review without bypassing controls.

5. Simulate a stale branch and validate the selected update or merge-queue policy.
6. Document the emergency-change path and perform a tabletop review without bypassing controls. Validation Evidence

Unreviewed changes cannot merge through the normal path.

The required check is evaluated for the exact merge candidate.

Pipeline configuration changes require the designated owner.

The repository records reviewer, checks, merge revision, and exception policy. Cleanup

Remove test bypass permissions and temporary accounts.

Retain sanitized screenshots or exported rule configuration as evidence. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. When is trunk-based development appropriate?
When teams can integrate frequently, maintain fast reliable tests, use compatible changes or flags, and keep
trunk releasable.

2. Why are long-lived branches risky?
They defer integration, hide incompatibilities, increase conflict scope, and create large hard-to-review releases.
3. What should a pull request explain beyond code?
Intent, risk, test evidence, rollout method, compatibility, data impact, and recovery.
4. Should administrators bypass branch rules?
Only through a narrow emergency process with strong logging, limited scope, and rapid retrospective
reconciliation. Chapter Summary

Git policy is part of the delivery control plane.

Prefer frequent integration and small reviewable changes.

Protect the exact merge candidate with reliable checks.

Emergency paths must remain exceptional and auditable.

Chapter 3: Pipeline Architecture, Stages, Jobs, Runners, and
Execution Isolation
A pipeline is a directed workflow executed by identities on compute. Good architecture separates
orchestration from execution, makes dependencies explicit, keeps jobs reproducible, limits privilege, and
preserves evidence across parallel and conditional paths. Learning Objectives

Design stage and job boundaries around evidence and failure isolation.

Use directed acyclic graphs, parallelism, matrices, conditions, and reusable pipeline components.

Select hosted, self-hosted, ephemeral, and isolated runner patterns.

Control concurrency, cancellation, timeouts, retries, and resource usage. Core Concepts
Workflow graph: Jobs should declare real dependencies rather than rely on accidental stage order. Independent checks can run in parallel; promotion depends on complete evidence. Job isolation: Each job begins from a known environment, receives minimum inputs, and publishes explicit
outputs. Hidden shared workspaces create non-reproducible coupling. Runner trust: Hosted runners reduce maintenance; self-hosted runners enable network or hardware access
but expand patching and persistence risk. Ephemeral runners reduce cross-job contamination. Reusable components: Central templates or reusable workflows standardize controls. Pin versions and define
inputs, outputs, permissions, and compatibility just like a software API. Concurrency control: Prevent overlapping production deployments or stale pipeline completion. Use
environment locks, cancellation of superseded runs, bounded parallelism, and timeouts. Failure semantics: Retries suit transient failures, not deterministic defects. Jobs must distinguish failed,
cancelled, skipped, unstable, and manually stopped outcomes.

uperseded runs, bounded parallelism, and timeouts. Failure semantics: Retries suit transient failures, not deterministic defects. Jobs must distinguish failed,
cancelled, skipped, unstable, and manually stopped outcomes. Reference Pipeline or Command Pattern
name: reference-ci
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
contents: read
jobs:
validate:
runs-on: ephemeral-linux
timeout-minutes: 10
steps: [checkout, lint, unit-test]
integration:
needs: validate
strategy:
matrix: {runtime: [current, previous]}
steps: [checkout, integration-test]
package:
needs: integration
outputs: {artifact_digest: sha256}
steps: [build, generate-sbom, publish]


Workflow components are pinned and versioned.

Timeout, retry, cancellation, and concurrency behavior is defined.

Artifacts and reports are passed explicitly, not through hidden local state. Troubleshooting Matrix

Hands-on Lab 3: Build a Parallel, Isolated Multi-Stage Pipeline
Prerequisites

A repository and CI platform supporting multiple jobs.

A small application with lint, unit, and integration commands.

A safe artifact store or workflow artifact feature. Implementation
1. Create separate validate, unit, integration, package, and evidence jobs.
2. Run lint and unit tests in parallel, then gate integration on both.
3. Use a matrix to test two supported runtime versions.
4. Publish test reports between jobs rather than sharing a persistent directory.

3. Use a matrix to test two supported runtime versions.
4. Publish test reports between jobs rather than sharing a persistent directory.
5. Add timeouts, cancellation of superseded pull-request runs, and a concurrency lock for a simulated


The job graph shows parallel independent work and explicit dependencies.

Each job succeeds on a fresh runner.

A stale run cannot overtake a newer environment deployment.

Published reports and artifact metadata identify the source revision.

Cleanup

Delete temporary self-hosted runners or revoke their registration tokens.

Remove lab artifacts according to retention policy. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why use a DAG rather than only sequential stages?
A DAG exposes true dependencies, shortens feedback by parallelizing independent work, and makes evidence
flow explicit.
2. What is the main risk of persistent self-hosted runners?
Cross-job contamination through files, processes, credentials, caches, or modified tooling.
3. When should a job retry?
Only for classified transient failures with bounded attempts and backoff, never to hide deterministic test or
policy defects.
4. Why pin reusable workflow versions?
An unpinned dependency can change pipeline behavior without a source change in the consuming repository. Chapter Summary

Pipelines are execution graphs, not long shell scripts.

Isolate jobs and pass outputs explicitly.

Runner trust and privilege are core security decisions.

Concurrency and failure semantics prevent stale or ambiguous delivery.

Chapter 4: Build Engineering, Dependency Control, Caching, and
Reproducibility
The build converts source into a deployable artifact. A trustworthy build has declared inputs, locked
dependencies, a controlled toolchain, deterministic or explainable outputs, safe caching, and provenance that
connects the artifact to its source and builder. Learning Objectives

Design hermetic or tightly controlled build inputs.

Use dependency locks, checksums, mirrors, and update automation.

Optimize caches without making them a source of hidden correctness or security risk.

Generate artifact digests, SBOMs, and build provenance. Core Concepts
Declared inputs: Source, toolchain, dependencies, build arguments, platform, and configuration must be
identifiable. Network access during builds should be deliberate and minimized. Dependency locking: Lock files and checksums make resolution repeatable. Version ranges alone allow
different builds from the same commit. Reproducibility: Bit-for-bit identity is ideal but not always practical. At minimum, explain non-deterministic
fields and prove that a controlled rebuild yields equivalent functionality and dependency graph. Cache design: Caches accelerate dependency downloads and compilation. Scope keys by platform and lock
digest, prevent untrusted branches from poisoning privileged caches, and treat cache misses as valid. Container builds: Multi-stage builds separate compilation from runtime, reducing final contents. Pin base
images by digest for controlled releases and rebuild regularly for patched dependencies. Build provenance: Record where, when, how, and from which inputs an artifact was produced. Provenance
supports verification but does not prove the source itself is safe.

es and rebuild regularly for patched dependencies. Build provenance: Record where, when, how, and from which inputs an artifact was produced. Provenance
supports verification but does not prove the source itself is safe. Reference Pipeline or Command Pattern
# reproducible build outline
SOURCE_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
LOCK_SHA=$(sha256sum dependency.lock | cut -d' ' -f1)
build --clean --locked --source "$SOURCE_SHA"
generate-sbom --output sbom.spdx.json
DIGEST=$(sha256sum dist/app.tar.gz | cut -d' ' -f1)
create-provenance --source "$SOURCE_SHA" --lock "$LOCK_SHA" --artifact "$DIGEST"
Production Checklist

Dependencies are locked and integrity-checked.

Build toolchain and base images are versioned or digest-pinned.

Untrusted changes cannot poison protected caches.

The build succeeds without undocumented local files.

Artifact digest, SBOM, and provenance are retained.

Hands-on Lab 4: Create a Reproducible Build with SBOM and Provenance
Prerequisites

A small compiled or packaged application.

A package manager with lock-file support.

Container or clean-runner capability and checksum utilities. Implementation
1. Pin the runtime or compiler and create or refresh the dependency lock file.
2. Build from a clean environment using locked dependency resolution.
3. Produce the deployable archive or container image and record its digest.
4. Generate an SBOM and a provenance statement containing source revision, builder, toolchain, and
dependency lock digest.
5. Repeat the build on a second clean runner and compare artifact or normalized-content results.
6. Add a cache keyed by platform and lock digest, then prove a cache miss still succeeds.

6. Add a cache keyed by platform and lock digest, then prove a cache miss still succeeds. Validation Evidence

The same source and lock resolve the same dependency graph.

No undeclared developer files are required.

The artifact digest and SBOM are linked to the pipeline run.

Protected builds do not restore caches written by untrusted code. Cleanup

Delete temporary build secrets and runner workspaces.

Apply artifact and cache retention policies while retaining required evidence. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why is a lock file important?
It records exact dependency resolution so the same source does not silently build against a different graph.

2. Is a reproducible build automatically secure?
No. It improves integrity and investigation, but reproducibly building vulnerable or malicious source remains
unsafe.
3. Why should base images be pinned by digest?
Tags are mutable; a digest identifies the exact content used for a release.
4. What is the danger of shared caches?
Untrusted jobs can introduce poisoned dependencies or outputs that privileged jobs later consume. Chapter Summary

A release artifact must be traceable to declared inputs.

Lock dependencies and control toolchains.

Caches improve speed but must not become hidden state.

Digests, SBOMs, and provenance strengthen artifact verification.

Chapter 5: Automated Testing, Quality Gates, and Test Evidence
Testing in CI/CD is a risk model expressed as executable evidence. Effective pipelines combine fast
deterministic checks with progressively broader tests, manage flaky behavior explicitly, and gate promotion
on results that are relevant to the changed system. Learning Objectives

Design a layered test portfolio for speed, confidence, and maintainability.

Separate unit, component, contract, integration, end-to-end, performance, security, and resilience tests.

Manage flaky tests without normalizing reruns.

Publish machine-readable reports and risk-based quality gates. Core Concepts
Test pyramid and portfolio: Run many fast isolated tests, fewer integration tests, and a small number of
expensive end-to-end scenarios. The right shape depends on architecture and failure risk. Contract testing: Validate interfaces between independently deployed components without requiring the
complete production topology. Contracts must be versioned and owned. Test data: Use deterministic factories, isolated namespaces, and safe synthetic data. Shared mutable datasets
create order dependence and privacy risk. Flaky tests: A flaky test produces inconsistent outcomes without relevant code change. Quarantine may protect
flow temporarily, but the test needs an owner, deadline, and visible risk treatment. Quality gates: Gates should use meaningful thresholds, changed-code scope, critical path, and trend. A single
coverage percentage is not a substitute for risk analysis. Evidence: Publish structured test results, coverage, logs, environment identity, dependency versions, and
failure artifacts with retention appropriate to audit and diagnosis.

entage is not a substitute for risk analysis. Evidence: Publish structured test results, coverage, logs, environment identity, dependency versions, and
failure artifacts with retention appropriate to audit and diagnosis. Reference Pipeline or Command Pattern

integration: [database, queue, external_stub]
release: [smoke, security, performance_budget]

critical_tests: must_pass

Production Checklist

Fast checks complete early and fail clearly.

Tests are isolated from order and shared mutable data.

Critical contracts and migrations are exercised.

Flaky tests have owners, deadlines, and tracked impact.

Reports identify source, environment, and tool versions.

Hands-on Lab 5: Design and Enforce a Layered Test Pipeline
Prerequisites

A sample application with at least one internal dependency or API.

A unit-test framework and machine-readable report format.

A disposable integration dependency such as a local database container. Implementation
1. Create fast unit tests for core logic and publish a structured report.
2. Add a component or API contract test with deterministic fixtures.
3. Start an isolated database or service dependency and execute integration tests.

1. What makes a quality gate useful?

It is tied to a known risk, uses reliable evidence, and has a clear corrective action rather than an arbitrary

2. Why are end-to-end tests insufficient?
They are slow, broad, harder to diagnose, and often fragile; lower layers provide faster, more precise feedback.
3. How should flaky tests be handled?
Make the flakiness visible, assign ownership and deadline, quarantine only when necessary, and measure the
lost confidence.
4. What should test evidence identify?

Testing is a portfolio of risk controls.

Use fast lower-level feedback and targeted release tests.

Do not normalize flaky reruns.

Quality gates must connect evidence to meaningful risk.

Chapter 6: Artifacts, Versioning, Registries, Promotion, and
Retention
The artifact is the unit of promotion. A mature pipeline builds once, assigns immutable identity, stores
metadata with the artifact, promotes the same digest through environments, and retains enough evidence to
reproduce or investigate every release. Learning Objectives

Define artifact identity with versions, digests, and metadata.

Use registries and repositories as controlled promotion boundaries.

Apply semantic versioning, release channels, and pre-release identifiers appropriately.

Design retention, replication, immutability, and rollback access. Core Concepts
Build once, promote: Testing and production must consume the same artifact bytes. Environment-specific
configuration is supplied separately at deployment or runtime. Version versus digest: A version communicates compatibility and release intent. A cryptographic digest
identifies exact content. Use both where possible. Semantic versioning: For a declared public API, increment major for incompatible change, minor for
backward-compatible functionality, and patch for backward-compatible fixes. Internal deployment identifiers
may use commit and build metadata. Registry controls: Separate write and read privileges, scan artifacts, enforce immutability for released
versions, replicate critical content, and log promotions and deletions. Promotion metadata: Record source, build, test, scan, approval, target, deployer, and verification. Promotion
changes status or repository location, not artifact contents. Retention and rollback: Keep artifacts and evidence long enough for operational recovery, legal requirements,
and vulnerability response. Test that older artifacts remain deployable with current configuration and
dependencies.

1. Why use both semantic version and digest?
The version communicates compatibility and release intent; the digest proves exact content identity.
2. What does build once, promote mean?
Compile or package once, then move the same immutable content through control states or repositories.
3. Should production deploy by mutable tag?
No. A friendly tag can select a candidate, but the resolved digest should be recorded and verified.
4. What determines artifact retention?





Chapter 7: Environments, Configuration, Secrets, Identity, and
Deployment Authorization
CI/CD crosses trust boundaries. Environment topology, configuration management, secret handling,
workload identity, approval, and deployment authorization determine whether a pipeline can change only
the intended target with the intended privileges. Learning Objectives

Design environment boundaries that support realistic validation without unmanaged duplication.

Separate application artifact from environment configuration.

Replace long-lived pipeline credentials with short-lived workload identity where supported.

Implement least-privilege deployment authorization and protected environments. Core Concepts
Environment purpose: Each environment needs a defined decision: developer feedback, integration,
performance, security, release qualification, or production. Duplicate environments without a decision create
cost and drift. Configuration separation: Store non-secret configuration as reviewed declarative data. Inject it independently
from the immutable artifact and validate schema and compatibility. Secret boundary: Use a dedicated secrets system, short-lived retrieval, minimal scope, rotation, and log
masking. Masking is not a guarantee that a secret cannot leak into artifacts or subprocess output. Workload identity: Federate the pipeline runtime to the target platform and issue short-lived credentials based
on repository, branch, environment, workflow, or runner claims. Protected environments: Bind production jobs to approvals, concurrency, allowed branches, deployment
windows, and specific credentials. Approval should evaluate evidence, not repeat automated checks manually.

2. What should an approval review?

3. Why separate build and deploy identities?

4. What is environment parity?

Chapter 8: Deployment Strategies, Database Changes, Feature
Flags, and Release Safety
Deployment changes running systems under uncertainty. Rolling, blue-green, canary, and recreate strategies
control exposure differently. Safe releases combine compatibility, progressive traffic, database discipline,
feature control, automated verification, and a practiced rollback or fix-forward decision. Learning Objectives

Select deployment strategy from availability, capacity, state, and risk requirements.

Implement progressive verification and automated stop conditions.

Design backward-compatible database and API changes.

Use feature flags with ownership, security, and retirement controls. Core Concepts
Rolling deployment: Replaces instances gradually. It is capacity-efficient but temporarily runs mixed versions,
requiring backward and forward compatibility. Blue-green: Maintains old and new environments and switches traffic. Rollback is fast when state and database
compatibility permit, but duplicate capacity and data synchronization matter. Canary: Exposes a small traffic or user segment first, compares health and business signals, then expands or
aborts. A canary without automatic analysis is merely a small risky deployment. Database expand-contract: Add compatible schema first, deploy code that tolerates old and new states,
migrate data, switch behavior, and remove obsolete schema only after all consumers are safe. Feature flags: Decouple code deployment from user exposure. Flags need ownership, targeting controls, audit,
tests for important states, and expiry to avoid permanent complexity. Recovery decision: Rollback is fastest when changes are reversible. Fix forward may be safer for irreversible
data changes. Define decision criteria before the incident.

1. What makes a canary effective?

Limited exposure, comparable telemetry, meaningful service and business signals, automatic analysis, and
automatic stop or rollback.
2. Why is database rollback difficult?
Data changes may be irreversible or incompatible with old code, so schema and application evolution must be
staged.
3. When is blue-green unsuitable?
When duplicate capacity is impractical, state cannot be synchronized, or database changes prevent old version
operation.
4. What is feature-flag debt?
Accumulated stale flags and alternate code paths that increase test combinations, cognitive load, and security
risk. Chapter Summary

Deployment strategy controls exposure but cannot replace compatibility.

Progressive delivery needs automated analysis and stop conditions.

Use expand-contract for shared data and interfaces.

Flags must be governed and removed.

Chapter 9: Pipeline Observability, DORA Metrics, SLOs, and
Recovery Engineering
A delivery platform is a production service. Teams need telemetry for queue time, runner capacity, pipeline
reliability, deployment flow, change outcomes, and recovery. Metrics should improve the system, not rank
individuals or reward unsafe gaming. Learning Objectives

Instrument pipelines with logs, metrics, traces, correlation identifiers, and evidence manifests.

Measure delivery flow and stability using current DORA-style metrics and supporting diagnostics.

Define CI/CD platform SLOs and error budgets.

Design recovery for runner, registry, pipeline, credential, and deployment failures. Core Concepts
Delivery performance: Track deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail percentage, and failed
deployment recovery time. Current DORA guidance also highlights deployment rework rate as an additional
signal. Diagnostic metrics: Queue time, job duration, cache hit rate, flaky-test rate, runner utilization, approval wait,
rollback rate, and artifact retrieval errors explain why outcomes change. Correlation: Carry source revision, pipeline run, artifact digest, deployment, environment, version, and
incident identifiers through logs and telemetry. Pipeline SLO: Examples include time to first feedback, pipeline availability, queue latency, successful artifact
publication, and recovery time. Error budgets guide reliability investment. Failure taxonomy: Separate source defect, flaky test, infrastructure outage, capacity exhaustion, dependency
failure, policy rejection, credential failure, and deployment health regression.

Chapter 10: CI/CD Foundation Architecture and Integrated
Capstone
The foundation capstone combines Git governance, isolated pipeline execution, reproducible build, layered
testing, immutable artifact promotion, protected deployment identity, progressive release, observability, and
recovery into one coherent delivery system. Learning Objectives

Design a vendor-neutral CI/CD reference architecture.

Implement a complete source-to-production evidence chain.

Exercise failure, rollback, and platform recovery paths.

Defend architecture trade-offs through a production-readiness review. Core Concepts
Reference architecture: Source repository, identity provider, runner service, dependency proxy, artifact
registry, policy engine, target environment, secrets system, telemetry backend, and evidence store form distinct
trust zones. Pipeline contract: Every stage defines inputs, outputs, identity, permissions, evidence, failure semantics,
timeout, retry, and recovery. Reusable components implement the contract consistently. Promotion model: Pull-request CI produces evidence; main integration produces a candidate; release
qualification approves exact digest; CD deploys progressively; verification records outcome. Independent verification: Deployment scripts should not be the only source of truth. External health probes
and telemetry confirm the target state and detect silent failure. Threat and failure model: Consider malicious pull request, compromised dependency, poisoned cache, stolen
runner token, mutable artifact, broad deployment role, registry outage, failed migration, and telemetry blind
spot. Production readiness: Review reliability, security, cost, performance, operability, compliance, evidence,
ownership, and recovery before declaring the system complete.

Appendix C: Production-Readiness Checklist

Source integration is protected, reviewed, and validated for the exact merge candidate.

Pipeline definitions and reusable components are versioned, owned, tested, and pinned.

Jobs run on isolated, patched runners with bounded network and least privilege.

Dependencies and toolchains are locked or otherwise reproducibly identified.

Builds produce immutable artifacts with digest, SBOM, provenance, and source metadata.

Test layers are reliable, isolated, risk-based, and publish structured evidence.

Protected caches cannot be written by untrusted execution contexts.

The same artifact digest is promoted through every environment.

Configuration and secrets are separated from artifact content.

Production authentication uses short-lived, target-scoped identity where supported.

Deployment strategy, compatibility, health analysis, and recovery are documented and tested.

Feature flags and database migrations have lifecycle and compatibility controls.

Pipeline queue, reliability, delivery flow, change outcomes, and recovery are observable.

CI/CD control-plane outage and emergency release procedures have been exercised.

All evidence is retained and sanitized according to policy. Appendix D: Ten Additional Portfolio Projects
